passage: "Eshaan, sit. You're worried about your friend Kunal, na? Let me tell you about my friend Suresh, forty years ago. He stopped coming to the tea stall. Stopped laughing. Said he had no reason to get up. Everyone told him, 'Cheer up, yaar.' That only made him hide. I didn't tell him to cheer up. I said, 'Come walk with me to the post office.' Ten minutes. Next day, I brought dal and rice and we ate on his step. Small things. Then I helped him book a doctor's appointment, and I went along. But hear this too. I had my own job, my own family. I couldn't carry him alone. When he once said something that scared me, I told his brother that same evening. That wasn't betrayal, beta. That was care. Suresh is still my friend today." Yogesh Chacha refilled Eshaan's glass of water.

qa.q: Where did Yogesh invite Suresh to walk?
qa.a: To the post office, for ten minutes.

qa.q: Why did Yogesh tell Suresh's brother when Suresh said something frightening?
qa.a: Yogesh was worried about Suresh's safety and knew he couldn't carry him alone.

qa.q: Which choice by young Yogesh helped Suresh start to come out of hiding?
qa.a: Instead of saying 'cheer up', he offered small things: a short walk, a shared meal, then help booking a doctor's appointment and going along.

qa.q: How might Suresh have felt when everyone said 'Cheer up, yaar'?
qa.a: He probably felt misunderstood and pushed away, which made him hide more.

grounding: An elder recalls supporting a friend with small doable actions, not demanding cheer, helping book an appointment, respecting his own limits and involving family over safety.

passage: It was the worst possible week: Jasleen had two exams and a project due, and only two hundred rupees left till her scholarship came. But Rekha, her flatmate, hadn't left her bed in three days. Jasleen didn't say, "Smile, it's not that bad." She said, "Walk with me to the chai stall? Five minutes." Rekha came, silent, in a hoodie. That evening Jasleen cooked one pot of dal and they ate it on the floor. She sat beside Rekha while Rekha booked a slot at the campus clinic. Then Rekha whispered, "Sometimes I don't want to wake up." Jasleen's heart jolted. She held Rekha's hand and said, "Thank you for telling me. I'm calling your sister now, okay?" Rekha nodded. Her sister came that night. Jasleen asked their friend Mehak to sit with Rekha the next evening, so she could sleep before her exam.

qa.q: How much money did Jasleen have left till her scholarship came?
qa.a: Two hundred rupees.

qa.q: How did Jasleen feel when Rekha whispered she sometimes didn't want to wake up?
qa.a: She felt shocked and scared; her heart jolted, but she stayed calm and held Rekha's hand.

qa.q: Which of Jasleen's choices protected both Rekha and herself?
qa.a: She called Rekha's sister at once over safety, and asked Mehak to sit with Rekha so she could rest before her exam.

qa.q: How might Rekha have felt when Jasleen didn't tell her to smile?
qa.a: Rekha may have felt accepted as she was, which made small steps like the chai walk and the clinic booking possible.

grounding: It shows a supporter who offers small actions like a walk and shared meal, does not demand cheerfulness, helps book an appointment, involves family over safety and minds her own limits.

passage: Ganga had been low for a month, barely leaving the Pune flat she shared with her cousin Ujjwal. He didn't tell her to cheer up. Instead, every evening at six, he knocked: "Chai stall? Ten minutes. You don't have to talk." Some days she came, some days she didn't. On Sunday he cooked rajma and they ate on the balcony. When she said she wanted help but couldn't face making the call, he sat beside her while she phoned the counsellor, and wrote the date on the fridge. He also knew his own limits. When he felt drained, he called his friend to vent, and he told Ganga, "If I ever get worried about your safety, I'll call your mother. Okay?" She nodded. "Okay."

qa.q: What did Ujjwal cook on Sunday?
qa.a: He cooked rajma, and they ate on the balcony.

qa.q: How might Ujjwal have felt on the evenings he called his friend to vent?
qa.a: He probably felt drained and tired from worrying, and venting helped him keep going without burning out.

qa.q: What did Ujjwal do that made his support wise?
qa.a: He offered small, doable things like a walk and a meal, never demanded cheerfulness, helped her book the counsellor and respected his own limits.

qa.q: How might Ganga see Ujjwal's promise to call her mother if worried?
qa.a: She may see it as caring and honest, and feel safer knowing someone is watching out for her.

grounding: Shows a supporter who offers small actions like a walk and shared meal, does not demand cheerfulness, helps book an appointment and respects his own limits, ready to involve family.

passage:
"Mehak, want to walk to the bakery? Ten minutes, that's all."
"I can't be fun today, Tejas."
"You don't have to be fun. Just come."
They walked. Mehak didn't say much. On the way back she said, "I keep thinking I should see someone. I just can't make myself call."
"Want to book it now? Online, together. I'll sit with you."
"Now?"
"Now. Then it's done."
They booked a slot at the student counselling centre for Tuesday.
"Tejas, thanks. I know I'm heavy to be around."
"You're not. But I'll be honest: I've got my own exams, so I can't be around every evening. I'll text at nine. And if I'm ever worried you're not safe, I'll call your brother."
"That's fair."

qa.q: When is Mehak's slot at the counselling centre?
qa.a: It is on Tuesday.

qa.q: How was Mehak feeling on the walk?
qa.a: She felt low and heavy, worried about being a burden and unable to be fun.

qa.q: What makes Tejas's support both kind and realistic?
qa.a: He suggested a small walk, didn't ask her to be cheerful, helped book the appointment, was honest about his limits and said he'd involve her brother if worried about safety.

qa.q: How might Tejas be feeling while supporting Mehak during exam time?
qa.a: Tejas probably feels caring but stretched, which is why Tejas sets clear limits like a nine o'clock text.

grounding: Shows a supporter offering a small walk, not demanding cheerfulness, helping book an appointment and setting limits while being ready to involve family.

passage: Last winter my best friend Ritu stopped answering calls. I'm Kashish, and I'd never seen her like that. I didn't know what to say, so I kept it small. Saturday mornings I'd bring aloo parathas and we'd eat on her steps. Sometimes we walked round the block once. I never told her to smile. When she said she'd tried to book a counsellor but kept closing the page, I sat with her while she finished the form. It wasn't all easy. One evening she said she didn't want to wake up. I didn't leave; I called her mother right then and waited with her till her mother came home. By January I was exhausted, and I started seeing a counsellor myself. Supporting someone doesn't mean carrying everything alone.

qa.q: What food did Kashish bring on Saturday mornings?
qa.a: Kashish brought aloo parathas.

qa.q: How did Kashish feel by January?
qa.a: Kashish felt exhausted, which showed the need to look after personal limits too.

qa.q: What did Kashish do when worried about Ritu's safety?
qa.a: Kashish stayed with Ritu, called her mother right away and waited until her mother came home.

qa.q: How might Ritu have experienced Kashish's small visits?
qa.a: Ritu may have felt cared for without pressure, since she didn't have to be cheerful to be with her friend.

grounding: Shows a supporter offering small doable actions, not demanding cheerfulness, helping book an appointment, involving family over safety and looking after their own limits.

passage:
Warden's note, girls' hostel, Block C.
Over the last two weeks I have seen Charu, from Room 14, quietly looking after her roommate Preeti, who has been missing classes and meals and staying in bed.
Charu doesn't lecture her or tell her to smile. Each evening she says, "Walk to the gate and back?" Some days Preeti says no. Some days she goes. On Sunday they cooked instant noodles together in the pantry and ate on the floor.
Yesterday Charu came to my office. "I helped her book an appointment with the campus doctor for Thursday. But I'm getting tired, and last night she said something that worried me." We spoke to Preeti together, and with her agreement I called her mother the same evening. Charu has also agreed to take a break this weekend with her own friends.

qa.q: Where did Charu and Preeti eat the noodles they cooked?
qa.a: On the floor, after cooking them together in the pantry.

qa.q: How was Charu feeling when she came to the warden's office?
qa.a: She felt tired and anxious, worn down from caring and worried by something Preeti had said.

qa.q: What did Charu get right as a supporter?
qa.a: She offered small, doable things like walks and shared meals, didn't demand cheerfulness, helped book the doctor, respected her own limits and brought in the warden and family when worried about safety.

qa.q: What might Preeti feel about Charu's quiet support?
qa.a: Preeti may feel trust and some comfort, since Charu stays close without pressuring her to be cheerful.

grounding: A warden notes how Charu supports her low roommate with small actions and a doctor's appointment, looks after her own limits and involves others when worried about safety.
